meta.title: AI adoption review checklist for hospitals
meta.description: Questions administration and nursing leaders can ask when a vendor proposes an AI product: purpose, regulatory status, patient data, security, performance, and operations.
meta.lead: Use this when you receive a specific proposal. Tick each item when you have a written answer. The items are the author’s list; the pages on data and records give the sections of 45 CFR behind many of them.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
items: The job the tool will do is described in one sentence and agreed by the department that will use it.
Who will use it, and who will be affected by its output, is listed (including nurses and front-desk staff).
The current process, and what measurement will show whether the tool helps, is written down.

sections.heading: Regulatory status
items: The vendor states in writing whether it treats the product as a medical device or as non-device clinical decision support, and why.
If it is an FDA-authorized device, the authorization pathway and intended use are written down, and you have checked that your use matches.
The vendor says whether there is a predetermined change control plan and what changes it covers.
You do not treat the FDA list of AI-enabled devices as proof either way, because FDA says it is not comprehensive.

sections.heading: Patient data
items: Someone has decided whether the vendor is a business associate, and a written agreement meeting 45 CFR 164.504(e) is in place before PHI is shared.
The vendor lists its subcontractors that touch PHI, and says where data is processed and how it is deleted.
The vendor’s planned use of your data, including any use to improve its own product, is stated and checked against the agreement.
If data is de-identified, the method (expert determination or removal of listed identifiers) is documented.

sections.heading: Security and incidents
items: The risk analysis was updated to include the new system.
Audit logs exist for systems that hold ePHI and someone reviews them regularly.
The contract sets a vendor breach-notice period shorter than the 60-day outer limit, and names a 24-hour contact.
The hospital’s incident record shows who decides and who files notices to patients, HHS and the media.

sections.heading: Performance and fairness
items: The vendor describes how the tool was tested, on which patients, and how that compares with your population.
You know whether the tool uses race, color, national origin, sex, age or disability as an input, and a mitigation step is recorded (45 CFR 92.210).
A plan exists to watch the tool’s performance after go-live, and a person who can switch it off.

sections.heading: Operations and people
items: It is clear what changes for nurses and administrative staff, and who gets additional work.
Staff are trained on the policy for the tool, and the training is documented.
The exit plan, including return or deletion of data, is written into the contract.
